entry: Maritime facility of one or more wharves or loading areas where ships load and discharge cargo and passengers. Ports are usually situated on a sea coast or estuary, but some lie far inland, such as [[Hamburg]], and reach the sea by rivers or canals. Ports carry 70% of global merchandise trade by value, and port cities often supply the labor for processing and handling goods. The greatest growth in port development is in [[Asia]], home to some of the world's largest and busiest ports, such as Singapore and Shanghai. One of the world's oldest known artificial harbors is at Wadi al-Jarf on the [[Red Sea]]. Ostia Antica was the port of [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]], with Portus established by [[Claudius]] and enlarged by [[Trajan]]. Dredging and spills affect water quality, and most port infrastructure is extremely vulnerable to sea level rise and coastal flooding caused by [[Climate change|climate change]].

Mass shooting on April 28, 1996, at Port Arthur, [[Tasmania]], Australia. Martin Bryant killed 35 people and wounded 23 others, the deadliest mass shooting by a lone gunman in modern Australian history. Most victims died at the Port Arthur Historic Site, and two at the Seascape bed and breakfast. Bryant pleaded guilty and received 35 life sentences without parole. The National Firearms Agreement, announced within two weeks of the massacre, restricted automatic and semi-automatic weapons and created a gun buyback, a national gun registry and a waiting period for firearm sales.

Port city and capital of Rivers State, [[Nigeria]], on the Bonny River in the oil-rich Niger Delta. It is the fourth most populous city in Nigeria, after [[Lagos]], [[Kano (city)|Kano]] and [[Ibadan]], with an urban population of approximately 3,800,000 as of 2025. Built by the British colonial administration in 1912 to export coal from [[Enugu (city)|Enugu]], the city became the center of Nigeria's oil economy after the first shipment of Nigerian crude oil was exported through it in 1958. Oil firms including Shell and Chevron have offices there. Oil spills, illegal refining and soot pollution from pipeline vandalism and artisanal processing have contaminated water sources and degraded farmland in surrounding communities. The city is highly congested, as it is the only major city in Rivers State.

Capital and largest city of [[Papua New Guinea]], on the [[Coral Sea]]. It emerged as a trade center in the second half of the 19th century. In [[World War II]], Imperial Japanese forces made it a prime objective in 1942–1943 as a staging point and air base. Royal Navy captain John Moresby first saw the site in 1873 and named it after his father, Admiral of the Fleet Sir Fairfax Moresby. Its population was 364,145 at the 2011 census and 756,754 at the 2024 census.

Capital and most populous city of [[Haiti]], on the Gulf of Gonâve. The bay, a natural harbor, has supported economic activity since the civilizations of the [[Taíno]]. The French colonial government first incorporated the city in 1749. Its layout resembles an amphitheater, with commercial districts by the water and residential neighborhoods on the hills, where rapidly growing [[Slum|slums]] cover the slopes. The city had an estimated 1,200,000 inhabitants in 2022; its metropolitan area had 2,618,894. In 1793, during the [[French Revolution]], colonial commissioner Étienne Polverel named it Port-Républicain, but it was later renamed Port-au-Prince again. A 2010 earthquake killed an estimated 230,000 people, according to the government. Since 2020, gang violence, including [[Kidnapping|kidnappings]] and massacres, has paralyzed the city.

Capital and chief port of [[Trinidad and Tobago]], on the Gulf of Paria. The city has been the island's capital since 1757 and serves as a retail, administrative and financial center for the [[Caribbean]]. It has the largest container port on the island, and [[Bauxite]] from [[Guyana]] is transshipped at Chaguaramas, about 8 km west. The pre-Lenten [[Carnival]] is its main annual festival. Trinidad and Tobago hosted the Fifth Summit of the Americas in 2009, attended by U.S. president [[Barack Obama]] and secretary of state [[Hillary Clinton]].

Most populous city in [[Maine]] and county seat of Cumberland County, on Casco Bay. It had 68,408 inhabitants at the 2020 [[Census|census]]. The peninsula was settled in 1632 as Casco and burned by the [[Royal Navy]] in 1775. The city was formally founded in 1786 and named after the English Isle of Portland. Its seal shows a [[Phoenix (mythology)|phoenix]] rising from ashes, recalling its recovery from four devastating fires. The Port of Portland is the second-largest tonnage seaport in New England. [[Portland, Oregon]] was named after this city.

Most populous city in [[Oregon]], U.S., at the confluence of the Willamette and [[Columbia River|Columbia]] rivers. It had 652,503 inhabitants at the 2020 census and is the county seat of Multnomah County. Following a coin toss, it was named after [[Portland, Maine]]. Its economy is driven by technology, athletic and outdoor brands, shipping and craft industries. [[Homelessness]] and property crime remain social issues, although recent trends show a relatively low violent crime rate. Portland is called the "City of Roses" and manages growth with an urban growth boundary.

Second-largest city in [[Portugal]], on the Douro River estuary, also known in English as Oporto. The municipality covers 41.42 sq km and had an estimated 273,476 people, while its metropolitan area had about 1.9 million in 2025. Its historic core, with the Luiz I Bridge and the Monastery of Serra do Pilar, was named a [[World Heritage Site]] by [[UNESCO]] in 1996. Settlement dates to the 2nd century BC, when it was an outpost of the [[Roman Republic]]. In 1415, [[Prince Henry the Navigator]] launched the conquest of Ceuta from Porto, initiating the Portuguese [[Age of Discovery]]. Port wine is named after the city, and cellars in Vila Nova de Gaia packaged and shipped the fortified wine.

Capital and largest city of [[Rio Grande do Sul]], Brazil, on the eastern bank of the Guaíba Lake. It has about 1.4 million inhabitants (2022) and is the center of Brazil's fifth-largest metropolitan area, with 4.1 million. The official founding date is March 26, 1772, and the city became the provincial capital in 1773. Its port and shipyards grew rapidly in the late 18th century, and it was the first city to implement participatory budgeting. It hosted the World Social Forum in the late 20th and early 21st centuries, and it was a host city for the 2014 [[FIFA]] World Cup and a venue for the 1950 tournament.

Artistic representation of one or more persons, the face predominant, in painting, photography, sculpture or other media. A portrait may show the subject in half or full length to convey likeness, [[Personality|personality]] and [[Mood (psychology)|mood]]. In photography, a portrait is generally a composed image of a person in a still pose rather than a snapshot. Early representations of individuals were mostly of rulers, often idealized, although some, such as [[Akhenaten]] and other [[Pharaoh|pharaohs]], are recognizable by distinctive features. The [[Moche culture]] of Peru produced some of the few ancient portraits that accurately represent anatomical detail. True portraits re-emerged in the late [[Middle Ages]], and [[Leonardo da Vinci]]'s *Mona Lisa* is one of the best-known portraits in the Western world.

Country in southwestern Europe, on the western [[Iberian Peninsula]]. Officially the Portuguese Republic, it also includes the Atlantic archipelagos of the [[Azores]] and Madeira. Its population is 11.4 million, and Lisbon is the capital and largest city. During the [[Reconquista]], Portugal was established as a county of the Kingdom of León in 868 and became a kingdom in 1179. During the [[Age of Discovery]], the kingdom built the [[Portuguese Empire]]. It became a republic in 1910 and a dictatorship in 1926. The 1974 overthrow of that regime enabled democracy, which was established in 1976. Portugal is a unitary republic and multi-party representative democracy, and a member of [[NATO]] and the [[European Union]]. A developed country, it has an advanced economy that relies chiefly on services, industry and tourism. Portuguese is the world's fifth-most spoken native language, with more than 250 million native speakers.

The first and longest-lasting of the European colonial empires, initiated during the [[Age of Discovery]]. Portuguese sailors explored Africa's coast from 1418–1419 in search of a sea route to the spice trade. [[Vasco da Gama]] reached [[India]] in 1498, and [[Pedro Álvares Cabral]] reached present-day Brazil in 1500. By 1571, a string of outposts linked [[Lisbon]] to [[Nagasaki]]. When [[Philip II of Spain]] took the Portuguese crown in 1580, a 60-year Iberian Union began and rival powers attacked the empire. Brazil, its most valuable colony, declared independence in 1822. The 1974 Carnation Revolution led to withdrawal from Africa, and [[Macau]] was returned to China in 1999. The Community of Portuguese Language Countries is its cultural successor.

Marine siphonophore often mistaken for a [[Jellyfish|jellyfish]], found in the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific oceans. It is a colony of genetically identical zooids that function as one individual. A gas-filled float keeps it on the surface while tentacles up to 30 m long hang below, delivering stings strong enough to kill fish and [[Crustacean|crustaceans]], and in some cases humans. Groups of up to 1,000 individuals drift with [[Wind|wind]] and [[Ocean current|currents]]. [[Carl Linnaeus]] first described it in the 10th edition of *Systema Naturae* as *Holothuria physalis*.

Ancient Greek god of the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses, one of the [[Twelve Olympians]]. He protected seafarers and guarded many Hellenic cities and colonies. His Roman equivalent is Neptune. In Bronze Age Greece he was a chief deity at Pylos and Thebes, venerated under the cult title "earth shaker". Homer reports that Poseidon received the sea by lot after Cronus was overthrown. In the *Iliad*, he supports the Greeks in the Trojan War. In the *Odyssey*, he punishes [[Odysseus]] for blinding his son, the Cyclops Polyphemus, delaying his return by ten years. According to legend, he lost the patronage of [[Athens]] to [[Athena]] and punished the city with a flood. In Plato's *Timaeus* and *Critias*, the legendary island of [[Atlantis]] was his domain.

Numeral system property in which each symbol's value depends on its position, as a power of a fixed base. The [[Hindu–Arabic numeral system]] is the most common today, a base-ten positional system in which each digit is multiplied by a power of ten. Earlier additive systems, such as [[Roman numerals]], give each symbol a fixed value. The Babylonians developed the first positional system, in base 60, whose legacy persists in 60 minutes in an hour and 360 [[Degree (angle)|degrees]] in a circle. Early Babylonian numerals lacked a true zero, so 2 and 120 could look the same. Binary, in base two, is used in almost all computers because it is easier to implement in electronic circuits. A radix point extends positional notation to fractions and to any [[Real number|real number]] with arbitrary accuracy. The notation made arithmetic far simpler, which led to its rapid spread in western Europe.

Philosophical school holding that genuine knowledge is either true by definition or derived from sensory experience through reason and logic. It rejects intuition, introspection and religious faith as ways of knowing. Modern positivism was first articulated in the early 19th century by [[Auguste Comte]], whose sociological positivism held that society, like the physical world, operates according to scientific laws. Comte ranked the sciences by exactness, from [[Mathematics]] to sociology, which he called the "queen science". Positivist schools later arose in [[Psychology|psychology]], [[Economics|economics]], logic and historiography, attempting to apply the [[Scientific method|scientific method]] to their fields. Since the turn of the 20th century, positivism has declined under criticism for its alleged scientism, [[Reductionism|reductionism]] and overgeneralizations. It also influenced Kardecism.

Antiparticle of the [[Electron|electron]], with the same mass and an electric charge of +1e. When a positron collides with an electron at low energies, annihilation produces two or more [[Photon|photons]]. Positrons arise from positron-emission radioactive decay, which proceeds through the [[Weak interaction|weak interaction]], or from pair production when a sufficiently energetic photon interacts with matter. In 1928, [[Paul Dirac]] published the [[Dirac equation]], and in 1931 he predicted an "anti-electron" with the electron's mass and opposite charge. Carl David Anderson discovered the positron in 1932 at the California Institute of Technology, using [[Cosmic ray|cosmic ray]] tracks in a [[Cloud chamber|cloud chamber]]. The discovery earned him the 1936 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics.

Predominantly French art movement that developed roughly between 1886 and 1905, from the last [[Impressionism|Impressionist]] exhibition to the birth of Fauvism. It emerged as a reaction against Impressionist concern with the naturalistic depiction of light and color. Its principal artists were [[Paul Cézanne]], [[Paul Gauguin]], [[Vincent van Gogh]] and [[Georges Seurat]]. Cézanne reduced objects to basic shapes while keeping Impressionist color, and Seurat developed pointillism, the systematic use of tiny dots of color. Post-Impressionists extended Impressionism while rejecting its limitations, emphasizing geometric form, expressive distortion and unnatural color, but they did not agree on a cohesive movement. Critic Roger Fry popularized the term, using it for his 1910 exhibition *Manet and the Post-Impressionists*.

sort_key: post world war ii economic expansion
entry: Long period of worldwide economic growth after [[World War II]], also called the Golden Age of Capitalism. It began in the aftermath of the war and ended with the 1973–1975 recession, which followed the 1971 collapse of the Bretton Woods monetary system and the closing of the gold window by [[Richard Nixon]]. The United States, the Soviet Union, Australia and Western European and East Asian countries experienced unusually high growth, together with full employment. Countries devastated by war grew strongly as well, including [[Japan]], [[West Germany]], [[Italy]] and [[France]], while relatively unaffected [[Sweden]] also grew considerably. The boom coincided with a larger series of global changes at the height of the [[Cold War]], including the welfare state and a nuclear arms race.

[[Mental disorder]] that develops after a traumatic event, such as [[Sexual assault]], domestic violence, war or natural disaster. Symptoms include intrusive thoughts or dreams about the event, distress at reminders, and avoidance, lasting more than a month. Most people exposed to trauma do not develop it, but interpersonal violence such as [[Rape]] carries higher risk than accidents. In the [[United States]], about 3.5% of adults have it in a given year, and 9% develop it at some point in their lives. Psychotherapy and medication are the main treatments, and SSRI or SNRI antidepressants are first-line, moderately beneficial for about half of people. [[Benzodiazepine|Benzodiazepines]] may worsen outcomes. The term came into use in the 1970s, largely through diagnoses of [[Vietnam War]] veterans.

Small adhesive paper issued by a postal authority to show that postage has been paid. It is affixed to mail and canceled with a postmark so that it cannot be reused. Stamps feature the issuing nation's name and a denomination, except in the [[United Kingdom]], where the monarch's image signifies origin. The first adhesive stamp, the Penny Black, was issued there on May 1, 1840, bearing a profile of [[Queen Victoria]]. Within three years stamps appeared in [[Switzerland]] and [[Brazil]], and by 1860 they were in use in 90 countries. The [[United States]] issued its first federal stamps in 1847, depicting [[Benjamin Franklin]] and [[George Washington]]. Collectors, who study stamps through philately, often buy them without intending to use them for postage, making stamps a source of net profit for the issuing agency.

Architectural style of the 1960s, a reaction against the austerity and formality of [[Modern architecture|modern architecture]]. Robert Venturi's 1966 book *Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture*, published by the [[Museum of Modern Art]] in New York, called for complexity, historical references and ornament over modernist purity. In *Learning from Las Vegas* (1972), Venturi and Denise Scott Brown urged architects to celebrate existing architecture rather than impose visionary utopias. Charles Jencks declared the "death" of modern architecture in *The Language of Post-Modern Architecture* (1977). The style flourished in the 1980s and 1990s through the work of [[Philip Johnson]], Charles Moore and Michael Graves. In the late 1990s it divided into high-tech architecture, neo-futurism, new classical architecture and deconstructivism.

Set of artistic, cultural and philosophical movements that arose in the mid-20th century as a skeptical response to [[Modernism|modernism]]. It emphasizes the instability of meaning, the rejection of universal truths and the critique of grand narratives. Its practice includes eclectic styles, performative irony and pluralism. In the 1990s the term came to denote a generally celebratory response to cultural pluralism, aligned with [[Feminism|feminism]] and multiculturalism. Its philosophical core drew on [[Jacques Derrida]] and [[Michel Foucault]], and Jean-François Lyotard defined it as "incredulity toward metanarratives." Critics argue that it leads to a nihilistic form of [[Relativism|relativism]] and supplants moral and political ideals with style and spectacle. Its influence persists in arts, architecture, literature, music and fashion.

Name for mined and manufactured salts that contain potassium in water-soluble form. The term derives from pot ash, plant or wood ash soaked in water in a pot, the primary source of potash before the Industrial Era. Potash deposits are evaporite beds left by ancient seas. In 2021, world production exceeded 71.9 million tonnes (about 45.4 million tonnes K₂O equivalent), with [[Canada]] the largest producer, followed by [[Russia]] and [[Belarus]]. Most potash is used as [[Fertilizer|fertilizer]]. [[Potassium]] was first derived in 1807 by [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]] of caustic potash.
